Ultimately, women won the legal right to vote and run for office on May 28, 1952. ___E:Eleni Skoura U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleni_Skoura)___ , again from ___E:Thessaloniki U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thessaloniki)___ , became the first woman elected to the ___E:Hellenic Parliament U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenic_Parliament)___ in 1953, with the conservative ___E:Greek Rally U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_Rally)___ , when she won a by-election against another female opponent.

Women were finally able to participate in the ___E:1956 election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1956_Greek_legislative_election)___ , with two more women becoming members of parliament; ___E:Lina Tsaldari U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lina_Tsaldari)___ , wife of former Prime Minister ___E:Panagis Tsaldaris U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panagis_Tsaldaris)___ , won the most votes of any candidate in the country and became the first female minister in Greece under the conservative ___E:National Radical Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Radical_Union)___ government of ___E:Konstantinos Karamanlis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konstantinos_Karamanlis)___ .

No woman has been elected ___E:Prime Minister of Greece U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Greece)___ , but ___E:Vassiliki Thanou-Christophilou U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vassiliki_Thanou-Christophilou)___ served as the country's first female prime minister, heading a ___E:caretaker government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caretaker_government)___ , between August 27 and September 21, 2015. The first woman to lead a major political party was ___E:Aleka Papariga U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleka_Papariga)___ , who served as General Secretary of the ___E:Communist Party of Greece U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_Greece)___ from 1991 to 2013.
In Hungary, although it was already planned in 1818, [citation needed] the first occasion when women could vote was the elections held in January 1920.
Iceland was under ___E:Danish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark)___ rule until 1944. Icelandic women acquired full voting rights along with Danish women in 1915.

___E:From 1918 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women%27s_suffrage_in_the_United_Kingdom)___ , with the rest of the United Kingdom, women in Ireland could vote at age 30 with property qualifications or in university constituencies, while men could vote at age 21 with no qualification.

From separation in 1922, the ___E:Irish Free State U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Free_State)___ gave ___E:equal voting rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_voting)___ to men and women. ["All citizens of the Irish Free State (Saorstát Eireann) without distinction of sex, who have reached the age of twenty-one years and who comply with the provisions of the prevailing electoral laws, shall have the right to vote for members of Dáil Eireann, and to take part in the Referendum and Initiative."]  Promises of equal rights from the Proclamation were embraced in the Constitution in 1922, the year Irish women achieved full voting rights.
However, over the next ten years, laws were introduced that eliminated women's rights from serving on juries, working after marriage, and working in industry.

The 1937 Constitution and Taoiseach ___E:Éamon de Valera U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89amon_de_Valera)___ ’s conservative leadership further stripped women of their previously granted rights.
As well, though the 1937 Constitution guarantees women the right to vote and to nationality and citizenship on an equal basis with men, it also contains a provision, Article 41.2, which states:

1° [...] the State recognises that by her life within the home, woman gives to the State a support without which the common good cannot be achieved. 2° The State shall, therefore, endeavour to ensure that mothers shall not be obliged by economic necessity to engage in labour to the neglect of their duties in the home.
In 1881, The Isle of Man (in the British Isles but not part of the United Kingdom) passed a law giving the vote to single and widowed women who passed a property qualification.
This was to vote in elections for the House of Keys, in the Island's parliament, Tynwald.
This was extended to universal suffrage for men and women in 1919.

In Italy, women's suffrage was not introduced following ___E:World War I U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I)___ , but upheld by ___E:Socialist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialism)___ and ___E:Fascist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fascism)___ activists and partly introduced on a local or municipal level by ___E:Benito Mussolini U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benito_Mussolini)___ 's government in 1925.  In April 1945, the provisional government led by the ___E:Italian Resistance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Resistance)___ decreed the universal enfranchisement of women in Italy, allowing for the immediate appointment of women to public office, of which the first was Elena Fischli Dreher.

In the ___E:1946 election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1946_Italian_general_election)___ , all Italians simultaneously voted for the Constituent Assembly and for ___E:a referendum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1946_Italian_institutional_referendum)___ about keeping Italy a ___E:monarchy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy)___ or creating a ___E:republic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Italian_Republic)___ instead.

Elections were not held in the ___E:Julian March U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_March)___ and ___E:South Tyrol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_South_Tyrol#After_World_War_II)___ because they were under ___E:Allied U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II)___ occupation.

The new version of ___E:article 51 Constitution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Italy#Political_Rights_and_Duties_(Articles_48-54))___ recognizes equal opportunities in electoral lists.

In ___E:Liechtenstein U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liechtenstein)___ , women's suffrage was granted via ___E:referendum in 1984 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Liechtenstein_women%27s_suffrage_referendum)___ .

In Luxembourg, ___E:Marguerite Thomas-Clement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marguerite_Thomas-Clement)___ spoke in favour of women suffrage in public debate through articles in the press in 1917–19; however, there was never any organized women suffrage movement in Luxembourg, as women suffrage was included without debate in the new democratic constitution of 1919.

Malta was a British colony, but when women's suffrage was finally introduced in Great Britain in 1918, this had not been included in the 1921 Constitution on Malta, when Malta was given its own parliament, although the ___E:Labour Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(Malta))___ did support the reform.

In 1931, ___E:Mabel Strickland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mabel_Strickland)___ , assistant secretary of Constitution Party, delivered a petition signed by 428 to the Royal Commission on Maltese Affairs requesting women's suffrage without success.
However, there had been no organized movement for women's suffrage on Malta.

In 1944 the ___E:Women of Malta Association U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_of_Malta_Association)___ was founded by ___E:Josephine Burns de Bono U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josephine_Burns_de_Bono)___ and ___E:Helen Buhagiar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Buhagiar)___ .
The purpose was to work for the inclusion of women's suffrage in the new Malta constitution, which was to be introduced in 1947 and which was at that time prepared in parliament.
The Women of Malta Association was officially registered as a labor union, in order to give its representatives the right to speak in parliament.

The Catholic church as well as the ___E:Nationalist Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalist_Party_(Malta))___ opposed women's suffrage with the argument that suffrage would be an unnecessary burden for women who had family and household to occupy them.  The Labour Party as well as the labour movement in general supported the reform.

An argument was that women paid taxes and should therefore also vote to decide what to do with them. Women's suffrage was approved with the votes 145 to 137.  However, this did not include women's right to be elected to political office, and the Women of Malta Association therefore continued the campaign to include also this right.
The debate continued with the same supporters and opponents, and the same arguments for and against, until this right was approved as well.

Women's suffrage and right to be elected to political office were included in the MacMichael Constitution, which was finally introduced on September 5, 1947. A politician at the time commented that the reform had been possible only because of women's participation in the war effort during the ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ .
Monaco introduced women's suffrage in 1962, as the fourth last in Europe.

In Monaco, Women's suffrage was not introduced after a long campaign – although supported by the ___E:Union of Monegasque Women U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_Monegasque_Women)___ , itself only founded in 1958  – but was introduced as a part of the new Constitution, alongside Parliamentarism, an independent court system and a number of other legal and political reforms.

Women were granted the right to vote in the ___E:Netherlands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands)___ on August 9, 1919.  In 1917, a constitutional reform already allowed women to be electable.
However, even though women's right to vote was approved in 1919, this only took effect from January 1, 1920.

The women's suffrage movement in the Netherlands was led by three women: ___E:Aletta Jacobs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aletta_Jacobs)___ , ___E:Wilhelmina Drucker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelmina_Drucker)___ and ___E:Annette Versluys-Poelman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annette_Versluys-Poelman)___ .

In 1889, Wilhelmina Drucker founded a women's movement called ___E:Vrije Vrouwen Vereeniging U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vrije_Vrouwen_Vereeniging)___ (Free Women's Union) and it was from this movement that the campaign for women's suffrage in the Netherlands emerged.
This movement got a lot of support from other countries, especially from the women's suffrage movement in England.
In 1906 the movement wrote an open letter to the Queen pleading for women's suffrage.
When this letter was rejected, in spite of popular support, the movement organised several demonstrations and protests in favor of women's suffrage.
This movement was of great significance for women's suffrage in the Netherlands.
Liberal politician ___E:Gina Krog U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Krog)___ was the leading campaigner for women's suffrage in Norway from the 1880s.

She founded the ___E:Norwegian Association for Women's Rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Association_for_Women%27s_Rights)___ and the ___E:National Association for Women's Suffrage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_for_Women%27s_Suffrage_(Norway))___ to promote this cause.
Members of these organisations were politically well-connected and well organised and in a few years gradually succeeded in obtaining equal rights for women.

Middle-class women won the right to vote in municipal elections in 1901 and parliamentary elections in 1907. Universal suffrage for women in municipal elections was introduced in 1910, and in 1913 a motion on universal suffrage for women was adopted unanimously by the ___E:Norwegian parliament U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Norway)___ (Stortinget).
Norway thus became the first independent country to introduce women's suffrage.

Regaining independence in 1918 following the 123-year period of partition and foreign rule,  ___E:Poland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Polish_Republic)___ immediately granted women the right to vote and be elected as of November 28, 1918.

The first women elected to the ___E:Sejm U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sejm_of_the_Republic_of_Poland)___ in 1919 were: ___E:Gabriela Balicka U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriela_Balicka)___ , ___E:Jadwiga Dziubińska U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jadwiga_Dziubi%C5%84ska)___ , ___E:Irena Kosmowska U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irena_Kosmowska)___ , ___E:Maria Moczydłowska U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Moczyd%C5%82owska)___ , ___E:Zofia Moraczewska U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zofia_Moraczewska)___ , ___E:Anna Piasecka U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Piasecka)___ , ___E:Zofia Sokolnicka U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Zofia_Sokolnicka&action=edit&redlink=1)___ , and ___E:Franciszka Wilczkowiakowa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Franciszka_Wilczkowiakowa&action=edit&redlink=1)___ .

___E:Carolina Beatriz Ângelo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolina_Beatriz_%C3%82ngelo)___ was the first Portuguese woman to vote, in the ___E:Constituent National Assembly election of 1911 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1911_Portuguese_Constituent_National_Assembly_election)___ ,  taking advantage of a ___E:loophole U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loophole)___ in the country's electoral law.

In 1931, during the ___E:Estado Novo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estado_Novo_(Portugal))___ regime, women were allowed to vote for the first time, but only if they had a high school or ___E:university degree U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_degree)___ , while men had only to be able to read and write.

In 1946 a new electoral law enlarged the possibility of female vote, but still with some differences regarding men. A law from 1968 claimed to establish "equality of ___E:political rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rights)___ for men and women", but a few electoral rights were reserved for men. After the ___E:Carnation Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnation_Revolution)___ , women were granted full and equal electoral rights in 1976.
The timeline of granting women's suffrage in Romania was gradual and complex, due to the turbulent historical period when it happened.
The concept of universal suffrage for all men was introduced in 1918,  and reinforced by the ___E:1923 Constitution of Romania U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1923_Constitution_of_Romania)___ .

Although this constitution opened the way for the possibility of women's suffrage too (Article 6),  this did not materialize: the Electoral Law of 1926 did not grant women the right to vote, maintaining all male suffrage.
Starting in 1929, women who met certain qualifications were allowed to vote in local elections.

After the ___E:Constitution from 1938 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1938_Constitution_of_Romania)___ (elaborated under ___E:Carol II of Romania U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_II_of_Romania)___ who sought to implement an authoritarian regime) the voting rights were extended to women for national elections by the Electoral Law 1939,  but both women and men had restrictions, and in practice these restrictions affected women more than men (the new restrictions on men also meant that men lost their previous universal suffrage).

Although women could vote, they could be elected only to the ___E:Senate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Romania)___ and not to the ___E:Chamber of Deputies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamber_of_Deputies_(Romania))___ (Article 4 (c)).  (the Senate was later abolished in 1940).

Due to the historical context of the time, which included the dictatorship of ___E:Ion Antonescu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion_Antonescu)___ , there were no elections in Romania between 1940 and 1946. In 1946, Law no. 560 gave full equal rights to men and women to vote and to be elected in the Chamber of Deputies; and women voted in the ___E:1946 Romanian general election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1946_Romanian_general_election)___ .
The ___E:Constitution of 1948 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Romania)___ gave women and men equal civil and political rights (Article 18).

Until the collapse of communism in 1989, all the candidates were chosen by the ___E:Romanian Communist Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Communist_Party)___ , and civil rights were merely symbolic under this authoritarian regime.

Despite initial apprehension against enfranchising women for the right to vote for the upcoming ___E:Constituent Assembly election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1917_Russian_Constituent_Assembly_election)___ , the ___E:League for Women's Equality U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/League_for_Women%27s_Equality)___ and other suffragists rallied throughout the year of 1917 for the right to vote. After much pressure (including a 40,000-strong march on the ___E:Tauride Palace U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tauride_Palace)___ ), on July 20, 1917, the ___E:Provisional Government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Provisional_Government)___ enfranchised women with the right to vote.

___E:San Marino U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Marino)___ introduced ___E:women's suffrage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_San_Marino)___ in 1959,  following the 1957 constitutional crisis known as ___E:Fatti di Rovereta U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatti_di_Rovereta)___ .
It was however only in 1973 that women obtained the right to stand for election.

During the ___E:Miguel Primo de Rivera U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Primo_de_Rivera)___ regime (1923–1930) only women who were considered heads of household were allowed to ___E:vote U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vote)___ in local elections, but there were none at that time. Women's suffrage was officially adopted in 1931 despite the opposition of ___E:Margarita Nelken U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margarita_Nelken)___ and ___E:Victoria Kent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Kent)___ , two female MPs (both members of the Republican Radical-Socialist Party), who argued that women in Spain at that moment lacked social and political education enough to vote responsibly because they would be unduly influenced by Catholic priests.

Most Spanish Republicans at the time held the same view.  The other female MP at the time, ___E:Clara Campoamor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clara_Campoamor)___ of the liberal Radical Party, was a strong advocate of women's suffrage and she was the one leading the Parliament's affirmative vote. During the ___E:Franco U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francoist_Spain)___ regime in the "organic democracy" type of elections called "referendums" (Franco's regime was dictatorial) women over 21 were allowed to vote without distinction.
From 1976, during the ___E:Spanish transition to democracy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_transition_to_democracy)___ women fully exercised the right to vote and be elected to office.
During the ___E:Age of Liberty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Liberty)___ (1718–1772), Sweden had conditional women's suffrage.
Until the reform of 1865, the local elections consisted of mayoral elections in the cities, and elections of parish vicars in the countryside parishes.

The Sockenstämma was the local parish council who handled local affairs, in which the parish vicar presided and the local peasantry assembled and voted, an informally regulated process in which women are reported to have participated already in the 17th century.
The national elections consisted of the election of the representations to the ___E:Riksdag of the Estates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riksdag_of_the_Estates)___ .
Suffrage was gender neutral and therefore applied to women as well as men if they filled the qualifications of a voting citizen.

These qualifications were changed during the course of the 18th-century, as well as the local interpretation of the credentials, affecting the number of qualified voters: the qualifications also differed between cities and countryside, as well as local or national elections.

Initially, the right to ___E:vote U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vote)___ in local city elections (mayoral elections) was granted to every burgher , which was defined as a taxpaying citizen with a ___E:guild U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guild)___ membership.
Women as well as men were members of guilds, which resulted in women's suffrage for a limited number of women.

In 1734, suffrage in both national and local elections, in cities as well as countryside, was granted to every property owning taxpaying citizen of ___E:legal majority U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_majority)___ .

This extended suffrage to all taxpaying property owning women whether guild members or not, but excluded married women and the majority of unmarried women, as married women were defined as legal minors, and unmarried women were minors unless they applied for legal majority by royal dispensation, while widowed and divorced women were of legal majority.
The 1734 reform increased the participation of women in elections from 55 to 71 percent.
Between 1726 and 1742, women voted in 17 of 31 examined mayoral elections.

Reportedly, some women voters in mayoral elections preferred to appoint a male to vote for them by ___E:proxy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proxy_voting)___ in the city hall because they found it embarrassing to do so in person, which was cited as a reason to abolish women's suffrage by its opponents.

The custom to appoint to vote by proxy was however used also by males, and it was in fact common for men, who were absent or ill during elections, to appoint their wives to vote for them.  In ___E:Vaasa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaasa)___ in Finland (then a Swedish province), there was opposition against women participating in the town hall discussing political issues as this was not seen as their right place, and women's suffrage appears to have been opposed in practice in some parts of the realm: when ___E:Anna Elisabeth Baer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Elisabeth_Baer)___ and two other women petitioned to vote in ___E:Turku U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turku)___ in 1771, they were not allowed to do so by town officials.

In 1758, women were excluded from mayoral elections by a new regulation by which they could no longer be defined as burghers, but women's suffrage was kept in the national elections as well as the countryside parish elections.
Women participated in all of the eleven national elections held up until 1757.  In 1772, women's suffrage in national elections was abolished by demand from the burgher estate.
Women's suffrage was first abolished for taxpaying unmarried women of legal majority, and then for widows.

However, the local interpretation of the prohibition of women's suffrage varied, and some cities continued to allow women to vote: in ___E:Kalmar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalmar)___ , ___E:Växjö U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%A4xj%C3%B6)___ , ___E:Västervik U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%A4stervik)___ , ___E:Simrishamn U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simrishamn)___ , ___E:Ystad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ystad)___ , ___E:Åmål U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%85m%C3%A5l)___ , ___E:Karlstad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlstad)___ , ___E:Bergslagen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergslagen)___ , ___E:Dalarna U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalarna)___ and ___E:Norrland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norrland)___ , women were allowed to continue to vote despite the 1772 ban, while in ___E:Lund U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lund)___ , ___E:Uppsala U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uppsala)___ , ___E:Skara U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skara)___ , Turku, ___E:Gothenburg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothenburg)___ and ___E:Marstrand U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marstrand)___ , women were strictly barred from the vote after 1772.

While women's suffrage was banned in the mayoral elections in 1758 and in the national elections in 1772, no such bar was ever introduced in the local elections in the countryside, where women therefore continued to vote in the local parish elections of vicars.

In a series of reforms in 1813–1817, unmarried women of legal majority, "Unmarried maiden, who has been declared of legal majority", were given the right to vote in the sockestämma (local parish council, the predecessor of the communal and city councils), and the kyrkoråd (local church councils).

In 1823, a suggestion was raised by the mayor of Strängnäs to reintroduce women's suffrage for taxpaying women of legal majority (unmarried, divorced and widowed women) in the mayoral elections, and this right was reintroduced in 1858.

In 1862, tax-paying women of legal majority (unmarried, divorced and widowed women) were again allowed to vote in municipal elections, making Sweden the first country in the world to grant women the right to vote.  This was after the introduction of a new political system, where a new local authority was introduced: the communal municipal council.
The right to vote in municipal elections applied only to people of legal majority, which excluded married women, as they were juridically under the guardianship of their husbands.
In 1884 the suggestion to grant women the right to vote in national elections was initially voted down in Parliament.

During the 1880s, the ___E:Married Woman's Property Rights Association U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Married_Woman%27s_Property_Rights_Association)___ had a campaign to encourage the female voters, qualified to vote in accordance with the 1862 law, to use their vote and increase the participation of women voters in the elections, but there was yet no public demand for women's suffrage among women.

In 1888, the ___E:temperance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperance_movement)___ activist ___E:Emilie Rathou U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilie_Rathou)___ became the first woman in Sweden to demand the right for women's suffrage in a public speech.

In 1899, a delegation from the ___E:Fredrika Bremer Association U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredrika_Bremer_Association)___ presented a suggestion of women's suffrage to prime minister ___E:Erik Gustaf Boström U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erik_Gustaf_Bostr%C3%B6m)___ .

The delegation was headed by ___E:Agda Montelius U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agda_Montelius)___ , accompanied by ___E:Gertrud Adelborg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gertrud_Adelborg)___ , who had written the demand.
This was the first time the Swedish women's movement themselves had officially presented a demand for suffrage.

In 1902 the ___E:Swedish Society for Woman Suffrage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_for_Women%27s_Suffrage_(Sweden))___ was founded, supported by the ___E:Social Democratic women's Clubs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholms_Allm%C3%A4nna_Kvinnoklubb)___ .
In 1906 the suggestion of women's suffrage was voted down in parliament again.
In 1909, the right to vote in municipal elections were extended to also include married women.

The same year, women were granted eligibility for election to municipal councils,  and in the following 1910–11 municipal elections, forty women were elected to different municipal councils,  ___E:Gertrud Månsson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gertrud_M%C3%A5nsson)___ being the first.
In 1914 ___E:Emilia Broomé U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilia_Broom%C3%A9)___ became the first woman in the legislative assembly.
The right to vote in national elections was not returned to women until 1919, and was practiced again in the election of 1921, for the first time in 150 years.

After the 1921 election, the first women were elected to Swedish Parliament after women's suffrage were ___E:Kerstin Hesselgren U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerstin_Hesselgren)___ in the Upper chamber and ___E:Nelly Thüring U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelly_Th%C3%BCring)___ (Social Democrat), ___E:Agda Östlund U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agda_%C3%96stlund)___ (Social Democrat), ___E:Elisabeth Tamm U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elisabeth_Tamm)___ (liberal) and ___E:Bertha Wellin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertha_Wellin)___ (Conservative) in the Lower chamber. ___E:Karin Kock-Lindberg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karin_Kock-Lindberg)___ became the first female government minister, and in 1958, ___E:Ulla Lindström U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulla_Lindstr%C3%B6m)___ became the first acting prime minister.

Groups looking to reform the 1936 Civil Code of Conduct in conjunction with the Venezuelan representation to the Union of American Women called the First Feminine Venezuelan Congress in 1940. In this congress, delegates discussed the situation of women in Venezuela and their demands.
Key goals were women's suffrage and a reform to the Civil Code of Conduct.
Around twelve thousand signatures were collected and handed to the Venezuelan Congress, which reformed the Civil Code of Conduct in 1942.
In 1944, groups supporting women's suffrage, the most important being Feminine Action, organized around the country.
During 1945, women attained the right to vote at a municipal level.
This was followed by a stronger call of action.
Feminine Action began editing a newspaper called the Correo Cívico Femenino, to connect, inform and orientate Venezuelan women in their struggle.

Finally, after the ___E:1945 Venezuelan coup d'état U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1945_Venezuelan_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat)___ and the ___E:call for a new Constitution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1946_Venezuelan_Constituent_Assembly_election)___ , to which women were elected, women's suffrage became a constitutional right in the country.

The right of women to vote has sometimes been denied in non-religious organizations; for example, it was not until 1964 that women in the ___E:National Association of the Deaf U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_of_the_Deaf_(United_States))___ in the United States were first allowed to vote.
The ___E:Pope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope)___ is elected by ___E:cardinals U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_(Catholic_Church))___ .
Women are not appointed as cardinals, and therefore, women cannot vote for the Pope.
The female Catholic office of ___E:Abbess U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbess)___ is elective, the choice being made by the secret votes of nuns belonging to the community.

The high rank ascribed to abbesses within the Catholic Church formerly permitted some abbesses the right to sit and vote at national assemblies – as with various high-ranking abbesses in Medieval Germany, who were ranked among the independent princes of the empire.
Their Protestant successors enjoyed the same privilege almost into modern times.

On 6 February 2021, ___E:Pope Francis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Francis)___ appointed ___E:Nathalie Becquart U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathalie_Becquart)___ an undersecretary of the ___E:Synod of Bishops U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synod_of_Bishops_in_the_Catholic_Church)___ ,  making her the first woman to have the right to vote in the Synod of Bishops.

On 26 April 2023, Pope Francis announced that women would be allowed to vote at the ___E:Sixteenth Ordinary General Assembly of the Synod of Bishops U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixteenth_Ordinary_General_Assembly_of_the_Synod_of_Bishops)___ ,  marking the first time women were allowed to vote at any Synod of Bishops.
In some countries, some mosques have constitutions prohibiting women from voting in board elections.

In Conservative Judaism, Reform Judaism, and most Orthodox Jewish movements, women have the right to vote. Since the 1970s, more and more Modern Orthodox synagogues and religious organizations have been granting women the right to vote and to be elected to their governing bodies.
In a few Ultra-Orthodox Jewish communities, women are denied the vote or the ability to be elected to positions of authority.
In the United States, Jewish women were hugely participatory in the suffrage movement.
American Jewish support started in the mid-1800s but grew significantly at the turn of the twentieth century due to Jewish immigration from Europe.

Jewish suffragists faced ___E:antisemitism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitism)___ and ___E:xenophobia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xenophobia)___ from ___E:anti-suffragists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-suffragism)___ and suffragists alike.
By the time of the ___E:Nineteenth Amendment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution)___ , a majority of American Jews supported suffrage.

___E:Ernestine Rose U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernestine_Rose)___ was a Polish American suffragist who worked closely with ___E:Elizabeth Cady Stanton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Cady_Stanton)___ and ___E:Susan B. Anthony U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_B._Anthony)___ .
